strengths: DRE-BO-SSL offers a reasonable combination of BORE-style classification with established label propagation and label spreading. Exploiting candidate geometry could be useful, and the method accommodates both continuous search and finite candidate pools.

The empirical comparison includes GP-EI/UCB and BORE/LFBO with several classifier families, using 20 repetitions and reporting standard errors. The results show substantial improvements on several synthetic functions and faster convergence on NATS-Bench.

The appendices provide useful sensitivity studies covering bandwidth, unlabeled-point counts, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling. Including a no-unlabeled-data comparison and reporting computational tradeoffs are valuable.
weaknesses: The central explanation—that semi-supervised learning alleviates overconfidence and improves exploration—is insufficiently established. Section 3.1 defines overconfidence through the spatial concentration of high class probabilities, but the supporting illustrations mainly show individual Branin trajectories. Expanding a high-probability region does not itself establish effective exploration. Quantitative measurements of exploration or local trapping, together with an ablation of random selection among flat acquisition maxima, would strengthen this claim.

The cluster-assumption argument is not justified by the sampling procedure. Truncated Gaussians centered on evaluated inputs need not produce high-density regions with consistent labels under the unknown objective and changing quantile threshold. Appendix C does not derive the claimed expansion of the favorable decision region and explicitly acknowledges that the cited i.i.d. semi-supervised learning bounds do not apply directly. Consequently, this discussion supplies intuition rather than theoretical support for the proposed sequential method.

The experiments do not convincingly isolate the contribution of unlabeled data. Figure 11 shows that removing unlabeled points can improve performance, notably for label propagation on Bukin6 and label spreading on Branin. Moreover, this ablation fixes beta at 0.5, whereas the main comparisons learn beta. A comparably tuned labeled-only kernel classifier on the main benchmarks is needed to distinguish benefits from graph propagation, bandwidth selection, and changing the classifier family. This matters because the principal methodological contribution is the addition of semi-supervised learning.

Important implementation details limit reproducibility and assessment of comparison fairness. The manuscript specifies L-BFGS-B but does not clearly explain acquisition maximization over the discrete pools, categorical encodings and feature scaling, or several diffusion and bandwidth-optimization settings. These choices materially affect the RBF graph. Section 4.1 also defines column-normalized transition probabilities but states P = D^{-1}W, a row-normalized matrix; this must be reconciled with the transpose in Equation 7.

The MNIST experiment provides limited evidence for the intended black-box optimization setting. Its representation comes from a CNN trained on 440,000 labeled three-digit examples to predict the exact quantity being minimized, achieving 96.9% test accuracy. A baseline that ranks candidates using this pretrained classifier is needed to assess the optimizer's additional value. The separate training and test construction is described, but extensive task-specific supervision makes this benchmark's implications narrower than the main presentation suggests.
